This study presents a novel, dynamic, and adaptive time-series model called Time-Dependent Poisson Autoregression, suitable for analyzing and forecasting count-based data over time. Our research indicates that this model system offers an optimal solution compared to traditional autoregressive models, allowing for parameter shifts in response to changing time-dependent characteristics of data. We discovered that a linear combination of historical forecasts, in addition to past data values, is essential for capturing complex patterns and relationships within count-based data. Furthermore, our findings suggest that typical statistical challenges, such as non-constant mean behavior and non-stationarity, are resolvable using the Time-Dependent Poisson Autoregression model. Methodological improvements enable the analysis of count-based data through dynamic, non-linear comparisons and evaluations. We also developed practical estimation procedures for model parameters, incorporating maximum likelihood estimation and a local linear approximation. Finally, we conducted a series of empirical studies on real-world data sets to verify the model's performance and effectiveness. Our results demonstrate the Time-Dependent Poisson Autoregression model's superiority over alternative models in forecasting and analyzing count-based data, as measured by mean absolute error and through dynamic panel data models. Therefore, this model offers a valuable tool for researchers and analysts working with count-based data. To address this issue, a new low-power operating mode called HyperDegrade Frequency was proposed, reducing CPU frequencies from GHz to MHz ranges. This research involves reconfiguring the CPU frequency hierarchy, where the HyperDegrade Frequency takes the highest priority, and implementing a new operating mode that utilizes a low frequency (currently 1.8GHz) for most tasks and reserves a high frequency (currently 3.8GHz) for critical ones. To evaluate the feasibility of this new mode, a prototype chip was designed and fabricated, demonstrating the HyperDegrade Frequency's effectiveness in reducing power consumption while maintaining performance. As a result, a working HyperDegrade Frequency was achieved, decreasing energy per operation by 15 times compared to existing low-power modes and improving performance per watt by 30 times. Furthermore, the research provides a set of practical guidelines for designing HyperDegrade Frequency capable CPUs. To further explore the potential of this new frequency, a set of performance per watt benchmarks were conducted on various CPU workloads, resulting in a 2.5 times improvement in performance per watt compared to existing low-power modes. The HyperDegrade Frequency's effectiveness was also evaluated on real-world scenarios, including video conferencing, web browsing, and office work, demonstrating significant energy savings of up to 80% without compromising performance. The HyperDegrade Frequency's potential was also analyzed on various future CPU technology roadmaps, forecasting a performance per watt improvement of 5 times compared to existing low-power modes and a reduction in operating temperature of up to 10°C. The research's findings provide valuable insights for CPU designers and manufacturers, offering a promising alternative to existing low-power operating modes and paving the way for more efficient CPU architectures. Observations have revealed a positive correlation between the black hole mass and stellar velocity dispersion in elliptical galaxies, as well as a similar, though less certain, negative trend between black hole mass and star formation rates in massive galaxies. However, at extremely high masses above $10^{11.0}$ solar masses, this relationship begins to reverse. To better understand this reversal, researchers have been examining the behavior of nuclear activity in massive galaxies. Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are believed to play a key role in regulating star formation through black hole activity, which could potentially explain the reversal observed in the black hole-star formation rate relation. Using a sample of 200 massive galaxies with accurate star formation rate measurements and black hole mass estimates, along with large-scale structural information, we investigated the connection between black hole activity, star formation, and the environment in which these processes occur. Our findings show that nuclear activity is more prevalent in galaxies with star formation breaking out around the central region and in those residing in dense galaxy clusters. These results suggest that environmental factors, which could trigger AGN activity, may also contribute to the formation of massive, low-density galaxies. This could imply that dust obscuration affects the observation of star formation in some of these galaxies, leading to an underestimation of their actual star formation rates and, consequently, the black hole-star formation rate relation. Therefore, we propose that both the intrinsic properties of massive black holes and the way these holes interact with their surroundings may be crucial factors in shaping the black hole-star formation rate relation. This view is supported by a theoretical model that accounts for the dynamics of gas and dust around black holes and the influence of environmental factors on galaxy formation. This model predicts a negative relationship between black hole mass and star formation rate for massive galaxies with high specific black hole masses, such as those found in dense clusters, and could provide a valuable framework for further research.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a mysterious internal angular momentum redistribution within a solar mass star, NGC 7099, after a massive asteroid belt was discovered around it. To better comprehend this enigmatic phenomenon, we've created a detailed model of NGC 7099's evolution, taking into account the possible ingestion of massive planetary bodies or alternative explanations for angular momentum redistribution. Contrary to expectations, our findings suggest the initial conditions of NGC 7099 were not unusually rapid or axisymmetric. Instead, we discovered a period of significant internal angular momentum redistribution around 10 million years ago, which could be caused by the ingestion of massive gas-rich planets or an unexpected process such as core overshot rotation. Due to the lack of observable signs of massive planets, we speculate that the most plausible explanation might involve the core overshot rotation of a massive stellar shock, leading to a disturbance in NGC 7099's core and subsequent angular momentum redistribution. To further investigate this theory, observations of NGC 7099's seismic modes with higher frequency resolution are recommended. 

The paper's findings could have implications for understanding the internal dynamics of similar A-type stars in the Milky Way and the Giant Molecular Shells observed around some of them, which may result from similar angular momentum redistribution events. Moreover, these findings could provide valuable insights into the formation mechanisms of rapid rotators among B-type and A-type stars, as well as the formation of massive planetary orbits around stars similar to the Sun.

A pervasive issue in medical image analysis involves a significant lack of labeled data, hindering the effectiveness of deep learning techniques. Semi-supervised learning has gained traction as a solution, incorporating labeled and unlabeled data to train models. However, it often relies on complex learning strategies, such as contrastive learning, which may not be efficient for all situations. Contrastive learning requires contrastive loss functions that often complicate implementation and may not be suitable for all datasets. In contrast, our proposed method, which we call Simple Unlabeled Data Regularization (SUDR), utilizes unlabeled data to prevent overfitting on trained models. This approach is remarkably straightforward, as it only involves ensuring that the model produces consistent outputs when fed the same input twice. Our results, obtained using standard semi-supervised learning methods and SUDR, demonstrated the effectiveness of this simple approach on three publicly available medical image datasets: BRAINS-EGFR, HPA-KID, and MMWHS. Our findings show that SUDR consistently yields comparable or better segmentation accuracy compared to contrastive learning, indicating its potential as a viable alternative. Code for the SUDR method is available at https://github.com/ChenXinyiZT/SUDR.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have achieved success in video identification tasks, but their effectiveness is compromised by their high computational requirements and large memory needs. This research addresses the performance issues of LSTM networks through an integrated design at the algorithmic and hardware levels, focusing on video identification using audio signals. A novel LSTM architecture called 'Hierarchical Tucker LSTM' (HTLSTM) is presented, which optimizes memory efficiency without performance sacrifices by employing a hierarchical tensor decomposition. This compact model enables efficient video identification on limited hardware resources. A hardware accelerator called 'Hierarchical Tucker LSTM Accelerator' (HTLA) is also designed to optimize the performance of HTLSTM by incorporating a tiered memory access scheme and a hierarchical tensor-based tile partitioning. The efficient video identification task was evaluated on the Creative Commons Attribution License SoundScenes dataset, which consisted of 20 categories, and the results showed that the HTLSTM model achieved high accuracy with a significant reduction in parameters. The HTLSTM model demonstrated area efficiency gains of 3.4 times over a base LSTM model and performance improvements of 3.9 times on a Xilinx Ultrascale+ VCU208 hardware platform. The research presents novel contributions in the areas of algorithm design, hardware design, and implementation, filling gaps in the existing literature. The results provide valuable insights for the development of efficient video identification systems using audio signals and offer practical guidelines for the design of compact LSTM models for other recognition tasks.
